Latent Bridge: Feature Delta Prediction for Efficient Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Model Inference

Abstract

Dual-system Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve state-of-the-art robotic manipulation but are bottlenecked by the VLM backbone, which must execute at every control step while producing temporally redundant features. We propose Latent Bridge, a lightweight model that predicts VLM output deltas between timesteps, enabling the action head to operate on predicted outputs while the expensive VLM backbone is called only periodically. We instantiate Latent Bridge on two architecturally distinct VLAs: GR00T-N1.6 (feature-space bridge) and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (KV-cache bridge), demonstrating that the approach generalizes across VLA designs. Our task-agnostic DAgger training pipeline transfers across benchmarks without modification. Across four LIBERO suites, 24 RoboCasa kitchen tasks, and the ALOHA sim transfer-cube task, Latent Bridge achieves 95–100% performance retention while reducing VLM calls by 50–75%, yielding 1.65–1.73×\times net per-episode speedup. Our code and checkpoints are publicly available11 1 https://github.com/1999Lyd/Latent-Bridge.

1 Introduction

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for generalist robotic manipulation, leveraging pretrained vision-language models to ground language instructions in visual observations and produce motor commands Brohan and others (2023b); Black and others (2024); Bjorck and others (2025). Among VLA architectures, dual-system designs—where a large VLM backbone produces a feature representation that a separate, lightweight action head decodes into actions—have achieved state-of-the-art results on diverse manipulation benchmarks. Unlike single-system VLAs that autoregressively generate action tokens through the LLM itself (e.g., RT-2 Brohan and others (2023b), OpenVLA Kim and others (2024)), dual-system VLAs (e.g., GR00T Bjorck and others (2025), π0.5\pi_{0.5} Physical Intelligence et al. (2025), Octo Ghosh and others (2024)) decompose inference into:

  1. 1.

    Stage 1 (VLM backbone): A vision encoder + language model processes the observation oto_{t} to produce features zt∈ℝN×Dz_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}. This is the heavyweight component and dominates inference time.

  2. 2.

    Stage 2 (Action head): A lightweight policy network decodes ztz_{t} into action ata_{t}, running significantly faster than Stage 1.

This decomposition creates a fundamental asymmetric latency bottleneck: the VLM backbone must execute at every control step, yet produces outputs that change slowly over time. For flow-matching action heads (GR00T’s DiT Bjorck and others (2025), π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s flow expert Physical Intelligence et al. (2025))—both sample the time variable from a Beta⁡(1.5,1.0)\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,1.0) distribution biased toward the data side—reducing denoising from ≥\geq10 steps to a single step incurs negligible performance loss in our experiments, making the VLM backbone the clear bottleneck. For real-time manipulation at 10–50Hz, this severely limits deployment.

Key insight: Feature temporal redundancy.

We observe that consecutive VLM outputs exhibit high temporal similarity, meaning each expensive backbone call produces features that are largely redundant with the previous timestep. This redundancy suggests that a much smaller model could predict the output delta Δt=zt+1−zt\Delta_{t}=z_{t+1}-z_{t}, allowing the action head to operate on predicted features while the VLM backbone is called only every ff steps.

Our approach.

We propose Latent Bridge, a lightweight model that predicts one-step VLM output deltas:

z^t+1=z^t+ℬ⁡(z^t,st,qt,at−1)\hat{z}_{t+1}=\hat{z}_{t}+\mathcal{B}(\hat{z}_{t},s_{t},q_{t},a_{t-1}) (1)

where z^t\hat{z}_{t} is the most recent representation (the fresh VLM feature on a VLM step, or the bridge’s own previous prediction on a chained bridge step), sts_{t} provides observation-dependent context (stable intermediate features or fresh vision embeddings), and qtq_{t}, at−1a_{t-1} are the robot state and previous action. Between periodic VLM calls (every f=2f=2–44 steps), the bridge chains predictions autoregressively, replacing the VLM backbone at orders-of-magnitude lower latency.

A bridge trained on sync data alone—rollouts collected with the VLM running every step, so the bridge always sees clean VLM features as inputs—learns from a clean-input distribution, but at deployment it must consume its own predictions during autoregressive chaining, creating a distribution shift that sync-only training does not cover. We close this gap with a task-agnostic DAgger pipeline: the bridge is rolled out in the simulator while the VLM runs in parallel to provide ground-truth feature targets along the bridge’s own trajectory, and the bridge is retrained on this mixed distribution. This pipeline transfers across all four LIBERO task suites without modification.

Our full pipeline therefore consists of three stages applied task-adaptively: Stage 1 is the bridge learning stage (sync collection + R0 supervised training + DAgger R1 refinement) and is the only stage required for simpler benchmarks; Stage 2 (LoRA action-head adaptation) and Stage 3 (phase-aware VLM scheduling) are added for long-horizon tasks where autoregressive bridge drift compounds over longer rollouts.

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Latent Bridge: a lightweight delta predictor that skips >>50% of VLM backbone calls on intermediate steps; orthogonal to and composable with existing VLM acceleration methods (pruning, quantization, layer skipping).

  2. 2.

    We instantiate the bridge on two architecturally distinct VLAs—feature-space for GR00T and KV-cache for π0.5\pi_{0.5}—and evaluate on LIBERO (4 suites), RoboCasa (24 kitchen tasks), and ALOHA sim (transfer-cube), achieving 95–100% SR retention with 1.65–1.73×\times net speedup.

  3. 3.

    A complete three-stage pipeline (bridge learning; LoRA action-head adaptation; phase-aware scheduling), applied task-adaptively—Stage 1 alone recovers near-sync performance on shorter-horizon benchmarks, and all three stages together fully recover synchronous VLA performance on long-horizon tasks—trained on a single GPU in a few hours.

2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action models.

VLA models combine pretrained vision-language understanding with action prediction for robotic control. Single-system VLAs—RT-1 Brohan and others (2023a), RT-2 Brohan and others (2023b), OpenVLA Kim and others (2024), and RT-X Padalkar and others (2024)—tokenize actions and generate them autoregressively through the LLM, inheriting its sequential decoding bottleneck. Dual-system VLAs decouple perception from action generation: GR00T Bjorck and others (2025) uses a DiT action head, π0.5\pi_{0.5} Physical Intelligence et al. (2025) uses an interleaved flow-matching expert, Octo Ghosh and others (2024) and HPT Wang and others (2024) use diffusion decoders, and CogACT Li and others (2024a) uses a continuous action decoder. Diffusion Policy Chi and others (2023) demonstrates that diffusion-based action heads achieve strong multi-modal behavior cloning. Our work targets the dual-system architecture, exploiting the separable representation between backbone and action head to skip backbone computation on intermediate steps.

Efficient VLM/VLA inference.

General VLM acceleration techniques include KV cache compression Li and others (2024b); Xiao and others (2024), speculative decoding Leviathan and others (2023); Cai and others (2024), visual token pruning Chen and others (2024); Bolya and others (2023), and weight quantization Lin and others (2024); Frantar and others (2023). VLA-specific adaptations span token pruning (VLA-Cache Xu and others (2025), SpecPrune-VLA Wang and others (2025), LightVLA Jiang and others (2026), VLA-Pruner Liu and others (2025), Compressor-VLA Gao and others (2025)), layer skipping (MoLe-VLA Zhang and others (2026)), and quantization (SQAP-VLA Fang and others (2025), DyQ-VLA Zheng and others (2026)), reporting 1.08–1.62×\times per-step speedups with various SR trade-offs. None measure net episode wall-clock time, and all still execute the full backbone—making them complementary to, not competitive with, our approach: rather than optimizing the VLM forward pass, we skip it entirely on bridge steps, and the bridge composes with any of the above on VLM steps that do execute.

World models and latent dynamics.

World models learn environment dynamics for planning or data augmentation. Ha & Schmidhuber Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) learn spatial (VAE) and temporal (RNN) representations; the Dreamer line Hafner and others (2020); Hafner and others (2023) trains policies via backpropagation through latent imagination; IRIS Micheli and others (2023) uses a discrete autoregressive world model with a transformer. In the visual domain, UniSim Yang and others (2024) generates realistic experiences via a generative model conditioned on diverse actions, and Genie Bruce and others (2024) produces controllable environments from internet video. LeCun’s JEPA framework LeCun (2022) and V-JEPA Bardes and others (2024) advocate prediction in representation space rather than pixel space, which is closest to our bridge’s operating principle. Our bridge similarly predicts future latent states, but in the VLM’s hidden representation space rather than a learned abstract state, and serves to accelerate inference rather than enable planning or representation learning.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

Consider a dual-system VLA with policy π⁡(at∣ot)=𝒜⁡(𝒱⁡(ot))\pi(a_{t}\mid o_{t})=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{V}(o_{t})), where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the VLM backbone and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action head. At each control step tt, the backbone produces features zt=𝒱⁡(ot)∈ℝN×Dz_{t}=\mathcal{V}(o_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} (NN: sequence length, DD: feature dimension), and the action head decodes an action at=𝒜⁡(zt,qt)a_{t}=\mathcal{A}(z_{t},q_{t}) conditioned on proprioceptive state qtq_{t}.

We seek a lightweight bridge ℬ\mathcal{B} that approximates VLM features without running 𝒱\mathcal{V}. We define the VLM call period ff: the backbone 𝒱\mathcal{V} executes once every ff control steps (i.e., at t=0,f,2​f,…t=0,f,2f,\ldots), and the bridge ℬ\mathcal{B} fills the remaining f−1f{-}1 intermediate steps. Equivalently, the VLM is invoked at 1/f1/f of the control frequency, so the VLM call rate scales as 1/f1/f. For example, f=3f{=}3 means 1 VLM call followed by 2 bridge steps, reducing VLM compute by f−1f=67%\frac{f-1}{f}=67\%. At intermediate offsets t′∈{1,…,f−1}t^{\prime}\in\{1,\ldots,f{-}1\} from the last VLM call at step tt, the bridge predicts:

z^t+t′\displaystyle\hat{z}_{t+t^{\prime}} =z^t+t′−1+ℬ⁡(z^t+t′−1,st,qt+t′,at+t′−1),\displaystyle=\hat{z}_{t+t^{\prime}-1}+\mathcal{B}\bigl(\hat{z}_{t+t^{\prime}-1},\;s_{t},\;q_{t+t^{\prime}},\;a_{t+t^{\prime}-1}\bigr), t′\displaystyle t^{\prime} =1,…,f−1\displaystyle=1,\ldots,f{-}1 (2)
at+t′\displaystyle a_{t+t^{\prime}} =𝒜⁡(z^t+t′,qt+t′)\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}\bigl(\hat{z}_{t+t^{\prime}},\;q_{t+t^{\prime}}\bigr) (bridge step action)

with the boundary convention z^t:=zt\hat{z}_{t}:=z_{t} (the fresh VLM feature on VLM steps), and where st∈ℝN×Ds_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} denotes stable intermediate-layer VLM features cached from the last VLM call, providing visual context without rerunning the backbone (Section 3.2). The bridge therefore chains autoregressively: at t′=1t^{\prime}=1 the input is the fresh VLM feature ztz_{t}; at t′≥2t^{\prime}\geq 2 the input is the bridge’s own previous prediction z^t+t′−1\hat{z}_{t+t^{\prime}-1}. This autoregressive chaining motivates the DAgger training stage (Section 3.3).

The simplest baseline is feature caching, which sets ℬ=Id\mathcal{B}=\text{Id} (i.e., z^t+1=zt\hat{z}_{t+1}=z_{t}, equivalently Δt=0\Delta_{t}=0), reusing stale VLM features on non-VLM steps. This corresponds to the zero-function bridge and serves as a lower bound; our learned bridge must outperform this trivial predictor.

The period ff controls the trade-off between speedup and action quality: larger ff reduces VLM calls but accumulates prediction error over more consecutive bridge steps. Our objective is to find the operating point that maximizes speedup while maintaining >>95% task performance retention.

3.2 Latent Bridge Architecture

Feature-space bridge (GR00T).

For VLAs with a single feature vector interface between backbone and action head, the bridge predicts one-step feature deltas via residual prediction:

z^t+1=z^t+Δt,Δt=ℬ⁡(z^t,st,qt,at−1)\hat{z}_{t+1}=\hat{z}_{t}+\Delta_{t},\qquad\Delta_{t}=\mathcal{B}(\hat{z}_{t},\;s_{t},\;q_{t},\;a_{t-1}) (3)

where z^t∈ℝNimg×D\hat{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\text{img}}\times D} is the most recent feature consumed by the action head (fresh from the VLM at a VLM step, or autoregressively chained at a bridge step; boundary z^t:=zt\hat{z}_{t}:=z_{t} as in Eq. 2), sts_{t} are stable-layer features providing scene context, qtq_{t} is the proprioceptive state, and at−1a_{t-1} is the previous action. The bridge ℬ\mathcal{B} is a Transformer with cross-attention (DiT blocks) consisting of:

  • •

    Self-attention over input features ztz_{t} with learned positional embeddings

  • •

    Cross-attention to stable context sts_{t}, providing visual grounding without a vision encoder

  • •

    AdaLN conditioning on (qt,at−1)(q_{t},a_{t-1}), injecting state and action information at every block

  • •

    Zero-initialized output projection, so the untrained bridge starts at the feature caching baseline (Δt=0\Delta_{t}=0)

Image-only processing.

Text-token hidden states are nearly invariant between consecutive steps (cosine >>0.9999) since the instruction is fixed within an episode, so predicting near-zero text deltas would dilute the gradient on image-token deltas. The bridge therefore operates exclusively on image tokens (Nimg≪NN_{\text{img}}\ll N) and copies text tokens from the last VLM cache; dropping text from the bridge input is safe because z^t\hat{z}_{t} was already produced by a text-conditioned VLM and implicitly encodes the instruction. Empirically this yields no SR loss while making the bridge sequence-length-agnostic.

Stable vs. dynamic layers.

We decompose the VLM’s intermediate hidden representations into stable layers (early/middle, cosine >>0.999 between consecutive steps) and dynamic layers (final, cosine ∼\sim0.95). The bridge predicts the action-head input ztz_{t} and consumes the stable-layer features sts_{t} as cross-attention context, which provide local visual context (spatial layout, object identities) for the current observation. On bridge steps, sts_{t} is reused from the last VLM call while ztz_{t} is freshly predicted.

3.3 Training Pipeline

Our training pipeline has three stages, all task-agnostic:

Stage 1: Sync data collection.

We roll out the pretrained VLA in sync mode (VLM every step) in the simulator and record tuples (zt,zt+1,st,qt,at−1)(z_{t},z_{t+1},s_{t},q_{t},a_{t-1}) along its closed-loop observation trajectory; bridge training is then fully offline on this fixed dataset.

Stage 2: R0 bridge training.

We denote the initial bridge trained on sync-only data as the “round-0” bridge (R0). The bridge is trained on sync pairs with a combined MSE and cosine loss, restricted to image tokens:

ℒ=‖z^t+1−zt+1‖2+α⁡(1−z^t+1⋅zt+1‖z^t+1‖​‖zt+1‖)\mathcal{L}=\|\hat{z}_{t+1}-z_{t+1}\|^{2}+\alpha\left(1-\frac{\hat{z}_{t+1}\cdot z_{t+1}}{\|\hat{z}_{t+1}\|\,\|z_{t+1}\|}\right) (4)

where all terms operate over image tokens only (α=1.0\alpha=1.0). Text token deltas are masked from the loss since they are near-zero and would dilute the gradient signal.

Stage 3: DAgger refinement (R1).

After R0 training, we apply one round of DAgger refinement to produce the “round-1” bridge (R1). The R0 bridge is deployed in simulation with VLM call period ff, while a VLM oracle runs in parallel to provide ground-truth features at every control step (the robot still follows the bridge policy’s actions). This yields DAgger pairs (z^t+t′−1,zt+t′)(\hat{z}_{t+t^{\prime}-1},\,z_{t+t^{\prime}}) for each bridge step at offset t′∈{1,…,f−1}t^{\prime}\in\{1,\ldots,f{-}1\} from a VLM call at step tt: the input is exactly what Eq. 2 feeds the bridge—which reduces to the fresh VLM feature ztz_{t} at t′=1t^{\prime}{=}1 via the boundary convention z^t:=zt\hat{z}_{t}:=z_{t}, and is the bridge’s own (potentially noisy) prediction at t′≥2t^{\prime}\geq 2—paired with the oracle’s ground-truth feature zt+t′z_{t+t^{\prime}} as target. The bridge is retrained on mixed sync + DAgger data, resuming from R0 weights with a reduced learning rate. DAgger is essential because at t′≥2t^{\prime}\geq 2 the bridge’s input is its own prediction, not a clean VLM feature; without DAgger, errors compound rapidly at higher ff.

3.4 Optional Enhancements

Phase-aware VLM scheduling.

For complex tasks with diverse motion phases, we dynamically adjust ff based on the previous action’s translation magnitude ‖attrans‖\|a_{t}^{\text{trans}}\|: high motion (‖attrans‖>τnav\|a_{t}^{\text{trans}}\|>\tau_{\text{nav}}) →f=2\rightarrow f{=}2, medium (τmanip<‖attrans‖≤τnav\tau_{\text{manip}}<\|a_{t}^{\text{trans}}\|\leq\tau_{\text{nav}}) →f=3\rightarrow f{=}3, low (‖attrans‖≤τmanip\|a_{t}^{\text{trans}}\|\leq\tau_{\text{manip}}) →f=4\rightarrow f{=}4. This allocates more VLM compute during high-dynamics phases where bridge predictions are less reliable.

LoRA action head adaptation.

When bridge features are significantly noisier than clean VLM features, we apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) Hu and others (2022) to the action head’s DiT, training on a 50/50 mix of bridge and sync features with Gaussian noise augmentation. This increases the action head’s tolerance to bridge prediction noise.

3.5 Adaptation to π0.5\pi_{0.5}: KV-Cache Bridge

Unlike GR00T’s single feature-vector interface, π0.5\pi_{0.5} Physical Intelligence et al. (2025) uses an interleaved design where the Gemma-2B backbone and Gemma-300M action expert share transformer layers: at each of L=18L{=}18 layers, action (suffix) tokens cross-attend to the backbone’s (prefix) per-layer KV cache. We adapt the bridge to predict pre-RoPE key and value deltas for all LL layers simultaneously:

{Δ​Kl,Δ​Vl}l=1L=ℬKV​(Δ​et,et,KV^t−1,qt,at−1),\{\Delta K_{l},\Delta V_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}=\mathcal{B}_{\text{KV}}(\Delta e_{t},\;e_{t},\;\widehat{\text{KV}}_{t-1},\;q_{t},\;a_{t-1}), (5)

where et=SigLIP​(ot)e_{t}=\text{SigLIP}(o_{t}) is the vision embedding, Δ​et=et−et−1\Delta e_{t}=e_{t}-e_{t-1} encodes what changed visually between steps, and KV^t−1\widehat{\text{KV}}_{t-1} is the most recent per-layer KV cache (fresh from the VLM at a VLM step, or autoregressively chained from the bridge’s previous prediction at a bridge step; same boundary convention as Eq. 2). ℬKV\mathcal{B}_{\text{KV}} uses a shared DiT backbone with 18 lightweight per-layer output heads. SigLIP (∼\sim5ms) provides fresh visual context far more cheaply than the full Gemma prefix (∼\sim46ms); total bridge-step cost is ∼\sim6ms with bf16 + torch.compile. Architectural details and RoPE handling are in Appendix A.

3.6 Inference

At deployment with VLM call period ff:

  • •

    VLM steps (tmodf=0t\bmod f=0): Run full backbone 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Cache ztz_{t}, sts_{t}, and KV pairs for bridge use.

  • •

    Bridge steps (tmodf≠0t\bmod f\neq 0): ℬ\mathcal{B} predicts Δ\Delta from the most recent representation—the fresh VLM feature ztz_{t} on the first bridge step, or its own previous output z^t′−1\hat{z}_{t^{\prime}-1} on subsequent steps (autoregressive chaining). The action head runs on the predicted z^t\hat{z}_{t}. Cost: 2–6ms vs. 46–63ms for the replaced VLM backbone.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Base models.

We evaluate on two dual-system VLAs: (1) GR00T-N1.6-3B Bjorck and others (2025), with an Eagle backbone (SigLIP2 + Qwen3) and DiT action head, fine-tuned per LIBERO suite; and (2) π0.5\pi_{0.5} Physical Intelligence et al. (2025), with a PaliGemma backbone (SigLIP + Gemma-2B) and Gemma-300M action expert, using the publicly released LIBERO checkpoint.

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on four LIBERO Liu and others (2023) suites: LIBERO-Spatial (10 spatial reasoning tasks), LIBERO-Object (10 object manipulation tasks), LIBERO-Goal (10 goal-conditioned tasks), and LIBERO-10 (10 long-horizon tasks, most challenging). We additionally evaluate GR00T on RoboCasa Nasiriany and others (2024) (24 kitchen tasks, different robot embodiment, zero-shot) and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on ALOHA sim Zhao et al. (2023) (bimanual transfer-cube task) to test cross-platform generalization. We run 3 random seeds ×\times 20 episodes per task unless otherwise specified (60 episodes per task; 600 episodes per LIBERO suite of 10 tasks).22 2 All datasets used in the paper were solely downloaded and evaluated by the university. All reported success rates are mean across the 3 seeds; the resulting run-to-run standard deviation is below 0.5pp on all reported configurations.

Hardware.

All latency profiling and inference experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU with bfloat16 precision and torch.compile.

Bridge models.

GR00T bridge: lightweight DiT predicting feature deltas (∼\sim2ms; no vision encoder needed on bridge steps). π0.5\pi_{0.5} bridge: DiT predicting KV-cache deltas (∼\sim6ms; includes SigLIP encoder for fresh embedding input). Ablation shows that a 19M-parameter bridge achieves identical SR to a 148M bridge; vision input and stable context are both critical for maintaining performance on harder, longer-horizon tasks (Section 4.4). Training: single GPU, a few hours per suite for R0 + DAgger R1.

Baselines.

We compare against FastV Chen and others (2024) and VLA-Cache Xu and others (2025) as token pruning baselines, along with feature caching (Δt=0\Delta_{t}{=}0). The majority of VLA pruning methods (VLA-Cache, LightVLA, VLA-Pruner, Compressor-VLA, MoLe-VLA, etc.) are designed and evaluated exclusively on single-system VLAs such as OpenVLA, where the LLM backbone directly generates action tokens. While SpecPrune-VLA Wang and others (2025) reports results on π0.5\pi_{0.5}, it is not open-sourced and involves extensive hyperparameter tuning (action-aware pruning thresholds, layer selection), making faithful reproduction difficult. In dual-system VLAs, the diffusion or flow-matching action head is sensitive to the dense conditioning provided by VLM hidden states or KV caches, making token pruning adaptation considerably harder than in single-system VLAs where such techniques are already mature. We select FastV and VLA-Cache as they are open-sourced and reproducible, and we adapt them to dual-system VLAs (GR00T and π0.5\pi_{0.5}) for fair comparison.

4.2 Main Results

Latent Bridge achieves 95–100% retention (avg 94.5% GR00T, 96.9% π0.5\pi_{0.5}) while feature caching collapses to 3–56% SR. Token-pruning baselines still run the full backbone: FastV yields net slowdown (0.95×\times) and VLA-Cache only 1.08×\times. These methods report ∼\sim1.3–1.5×\times on single-system VLAs, but on dual-system VLAs the speedup only affects the backbone fraction (60–70% of per-step cost), driving the net gain to a low Amdahl ceiling (Appendix H). Latent Bridge skips the backbone entirely—replacing a 46–63 ms VLM call with a 2–6 ms bridge—yielding 1.65–1.73×\times net speedup despite slightly longer episodes (+5–6%).

4.3 Cross-Benchmark Evaluation

We evaluate on two additional benchmarks beyond LIBERO to test cross-platform generalization: (1) RoboCasa Nasiriany and others (2024) with GR00T-N1.6-3B (pretrained checkpoint without task-specific finetuning), covering 24 kitchen tasks (door/drawer articulation, appliance control, coffee, pick-and-place) on the Panda robot; and (2) ALOHA sim transfer-cube Zhao et al. (2023) with π0.5\pi_{0.5} fine-tuned from the pretrained base, testing the KV bridge on a bimanual 14-DoF setup. Both use the same training pipeline as LIBERO (sync data collection, R0 bridge training, optional R1 DAgger refinement).

Bridge retention is 95.38% on RoboCasa (24 kitchen tasks) and 97.73% on ALOHA (bimanual), versus 75.17% and 52.27% for caching—++13.38pp and ++40.00pp gaps, largest on precise-manipulation tasks. Latent Bridge therefore transfers across embodiments (Panda, ALOHA bimanual), action spaces (7- vs. 14-DoF), and task distributions with the same pipeline.

4.4 Ablation Studies

All ablations use the π0.5\pi_{0.5} KV bridge on LIBERO suites with 1-step denoise unless otherwise noted.

Vision input.

We ablate the fresh vision embedding Δ​et\Delta e_{t} by zeroing it during training, forcing the bridge to predict purely from previous KV cache, state, and action.

Both vision and stable context are important, with degradation scaling with task complexity. Removing vision degrades Goal by −-11.16pp and LIBERO-10 by −-28.34pp; removing stable context degrades Goal by −-5.16pp and LIBERO-10 by −-11.00pp, as the bridge loses its anchor representation of slowly-changing scene structure. The 19M bridge matches or slightly exceeds the 148M bridge, confirming capacity is not the bottleneck.

DAgger training progression.

We evaluate the effect of DAgger (online distribution correction) by comparing R0 (sync-only training) against R1 (+DAgger fine-tuning) across all suites.

DAgger delivers consistent gains: ++4pp on π0.5\pi_{0.5} and ++4–13pp on GR00T, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks where autoregressive drift accumulates. R0 alone recovers ∼\sim93–96% of sync SR on the three easier LIBERO suites; R1 pushes retention to 97–100%. For GR00T LIBERO-10, Stages 2–3 (§3.4) further lift R1 67.17% →\to 73.17% (Stage 2 LoRA) →\to 89.17% (Stage 3 phase-aware), a ++34.84pp total gain; on shorter-horizon suites these stages are within seed noise, so Stage 1 alone suffices.

VLM call period vs. performance.

Figure 4 shows π0.5\pi_{0.5} SR across all four LIBERO suites as the VLM call period ff varies from 1 (sync, every step) to 12. Spatial, Object, and Goal stay above 94.5% through f=8f{=}8; LIBERO-10 degrades more steeply (94.0% →\to 84.5% at f=8f{=}8) due to long-horizon error compounding. The default f=4f{=}4 gives 75% VLM savings with <<1pp average SR drop; f=5​–​6f{=}5\text{--}6 is viable for shorter-horizon tasks.

4.5 Case Study: Why Caching Fails

On a representative LIBERO-Spatial episode at f=3f{=}3, caching’s KV cosine to ground truth drops to ∼\sim0.91 in a sawtooth pattern as the robot moves, while the bridge stays at ∼\sim0.99 (Fig. 5a); the resulting off-distribution features push the action head off-trajectory and task fails (Fig. 5b). A cached KV encodes only the stale scene, whereas the bridge actively predicts the update from cheap signals—SigLIP delta (∼\sim5ms), state, and previous action—closing the gap with minimal cost.

5 Conclusion

Latent Bridge predicts VLM output deltas for efficient dual-system VLA inference. Instantiated on GR00T (feature-space) and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (KV-cache), it achieves 95–100% SR retention with 50–75% VLM savings and 1.65–1.73×\times net speedup across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and ALOHA sim, via a three-stage task-adaptive pipeline (Stage 1 alone suffices on shorter-horizon benchmarks; Stages 2–3 close the gap on long-horizon tasks) and no changes to the pretrained VLA.

Limitations and future work.

DAgger requires online simulation, and the bridge is VLA-checkpoint specific. For interleaved architectures like π0.5\pi_{0.5}, the action expert still traverses all 18 layers, leaving a ∼\sim30ms denoising floor; suffix-level bridging via consistency distillation Song and others (2023) could push speedup beyond 2×\times.

Appendix A Implementation Details

Bridge architecture hyperparameters.

Both VLA variants use the same DiT backbone with AdaLN conditioning. Table 5 lists the key hyperparameters.

Training hyperparameters.

All bridges are trained with AdamW (weight decay 10−410^{-4}), cosine LR schedule, and gradient clipping at norm 1.0. Key hyperparameters:

  • •

    R0 (sync-only): learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, 200 epochs (GR00T) / 50 epochs (π0.5\pi_{0.5}), batch size 64 (GR00T) / 4 (π0.5\pi_{0.5}).

  • •

    R1 (DAgger refinement): resumed from R0 weights with --reset_best (best val cos reset to 0). Learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} for GR00T Goal (T_max=16), 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} for LIBERO-10 DAgger (LR 10×\times lower to stabilize long-horizon distribution shift).

  • •

    Loss: ℒ=‖z^t+1−zt+1‖2+(1−cos⁡(z^t+1,zt+1))\mathcal{L}=\|\hat{z}_{t+1}-z_{t+1}\|^{2}+(1-\cos(\hat{z}_{t+1},z_{t+1})), restricted to image tokens.

Data collection.

Sync data is collected by deploying the VLA in sync mode (VLM every step):

  • •

    GR00T: 300 sync episodes per LIBERO suite (≈\approx4,500–6,600 inference samples after filtering).

  • •

    π0.5\pi_{0.5}: 300 sync episodes per suite, 50 episodes for ALOHA.

  • •

    DAgger data (R1): 300 episodes of bridge rollout with VLM oracle labels, collected at f=3f{=}3.

Hardware and runtime.

All training and inference use a single NVIDIA A100 80GB with bfloat16 and torch.compile(mode=‘‘max-autotune’’). Bridge training completes in 2–4 hours per suite. End-to-end pipeline (sync collection + R0 training + DAgger collection + R1 training) takes roughly 8–12 hours per suite on a single GPU.

π0.5\pi_{0.5} KV bridge: architecture and RoPE handling.

Given the flattened per-layer KV cache KVt−1∈ℝS×(18⋅512)\text{KV}_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times(18\cdot 512)} (256 pre-RoPE K + 256 V per layer, flattened along the layer dimension), embedding delta Δ​et\Delta e_{t}, and current embedding ete_{t}, the bridge computes:

K^l,t=Kl,t−1+Δ​Kl,V^l,t=Vl,t−1+Δ​Vl.\hat{K}_{l,t}=K_{l,t-1}+\Delta K_{l},\qquad\hat{V}_{l,t}=V_{l,t-1}+\Delta V_{l}.

Δ​et\Delta e_{t} is projected and added to the KV input as a residual signal of “what changed visually”; ete_{t} serves as cross-attention context. RoPE is applied to K^l,t\hat{K}_{l,t} after prediction: since RoPE is a deterministic position-dependent rotation, we extract pre-RoPE K from the model’s post-RoPE cache via the inverse rotation kpre=kpostcos−rotate_half(kpost)sink_{\text{pre}}=k_{\text{post}}\cos-\text{rotate\_half}(k_{\text{post}})\sin, predict pre-RoPE deltas, then re-apply RoPE before reinserting into the cache. The output head for each layer is a lightweight LayerNorm + Linear mapping the shared DiT hidden state (d=768d{=}768) to a 512-dim vector (K delta concatenated with V delta); all output heads are zero-initialized so the untrained bridge starts at the copy baseline Δ=0\Delta{=}0. This 18-head design amortizes the DiT backbone cost across all layers while letting each head specialize in its layer’s dynamics.

Appendix C Bridge Quality Analysis

Validation cosine during training.

The R0 bridge converges within 30–50 epochs to ∼\sim0.97 per-token cosine on held-out sync data (image tokens, averaged over layers for π0.5\pi_{0.5}). R1 (DAgger fine-tuning) resumes from R0 and converges rapidly in 10–16 epochs, adding only 0.002–0.005 in cosine but translating to 3–13pp SR gains in closed-loop simulation. LR 10×\times lower (3×10−53\times 10^{-5}) is required for GR00T LIBERO-10 DAgger to avoid collapse; shorter-horizon suites tolerate the full LR.

Per-layer KV prediction quality (π0.5\pi_{0.5}).

The π0.5\pi_{0.5} bridge predicts pre-RoPE K and V for all 18 Gemma layers. Table 8 reports per-token cosine on held-out sync data. Early layers (L0–L5) are easiest to predict (cos 0.999+) because their KV depends mostly on the (fixed) text prompt; later layers (L10–L17) encode more observation-dependent content and are harder.

Error compounding across bridge offsets.

The bridge chains predictions autoregressively: at bridge offset kk, the input is the bridge’s own prediction from k−1k-1 steps back. Table 9 shows that chained prediction cosine degrades gracefully—explaining why SR remains stable at moderate ff.

Appendix D Full Frequency Sweep

Table 10 presents the complete frequency sweep for π0.5\pi_{0.5} across all four LIBERO suites (the data visualized in Figure 4). Spatial, Object, and Goal retain >>94% SR through f=8f{=}8; LIBERO-10 degrades earlier due to longer episodes compounding bridge drift.

Appendix E Latency Breakdown

Component-wise latency on A100 80GB with bfloat16 and torch.compile. Values measured with GPU warmup (first 5 calls excluded).

Effect of bf16 and torch.compile.

Without optimization, the π0.5\pi_{0.5} KV bridge runs at 16.6ms per call (fp32, eager attention). Casting to bfloat16 reduces this to 6.0ms. Adding torch.compile(mode=‘‘max-autotune’’) further drops it to 1ms for the bridge model alone (total bridge-step cost 6ms including the 5ms SigLIP forward). The bf16 + compile stack is required to achieve the reported 1.65×\times net speedup.

Appendix F Additional Ablations

Sync + DAgger data mixing.

R1 training concatenates the sync dataset (from Stage 1) with the DAgger dataset (from Stage 3) at their natural sizes (no reweighting). Table 12 ablates this choice.

Epoch count and LR schedule.

DAgger R1 fine-tuning uses cosine LR decay with Tmax=16T_{\text{max}}{=}16 for GR00T Goal and Tmax=100T_{\text{max}}{=}100 for LIBERO-10 (longer horizon requires more gentle adaptation). Shorter schedules fail to close the distribution gap; longer schedules risk over-fitting to DAgger noise.

Appendix G Transferability

Cross-suite bridge transfer (π0.5\pi_{0.5}).

We test whether a bridge trained on one LIBERO suite transfers zero-shot to others. Table 13 shows that the Spatial bridge partially transfers to Object (94.0%) but degrades on Goal (79.0%) and LIBERO-10 (77.5%). Bridges learn suite-specific scene dynamics, supporting the need for per-suite training (bridge training is fast—a few hours per suite on a single GPU).

RoboCasa 12-task →\rightarrow 24-task transfer (GR00T).

We also test transfer within RoboCasa: train bridge on 12 tasks, evaluate on held-out 12. The bridge achieves 58.1% SR on held-out tasks (sync: 63.4%), a 91.6% retention, confirming partial within-benchmark generalization across task categories.

Appendix H Baseline Implementation Details

Token-pruning baselines (FastV, VLA-Cache) were originally designed and evaluated on single-system VLAs (e.g., OpenVLA) where the LLM backbone autoregressively generates action tokens. We re-implemented both from their official repositories and adapted them to the dual-system architectures studied here. We document below the full adaptation choices, hyperparameters, and failure modes.

FastV adaptation.

FastV Chen and others [2024] performs early-layer attention-based visual token pruning.

Hyperparameters. We use the default FastV configuration from the original paper: prune ratio R=0.5R=0.5 (drop 50% of image tokens) at layer K=2K=2, selecting tokens by average attention weight from all text tokens to each image token across the first KK layers. We also swept R∈{0.25,0.50,0.75}R\in\{0.25,0.50,0.75\} and K∈{2,4,6}K\in\{2,4,6\} per VLA and report the best SR configuration in the main table (R=0.5R{=}0.5, K=2K{=}2 in both cases); more aggressive pruning (e.g., R=0.75R{=}0.75 at K=2K{=}2) collapsed SR to <<20%.

Integration point. For GR00T-N1.6-3B, pruning is applied on the Qwen3 LLM side (after the SigLIP2 vision encoder + projection), at transformer layer 2. For π0.5\pi_{0.5}, pruning is applied in the PaliGemma prefix computation at Gemma layer 2. In both cases the action head still receives the full-length hidden state (pruned tokens masked with zero) at the interface layer so that the pre-trained interface between backbone and action head is not re-shaped.

Why SR degrades. Dual-system action heads attend densely to all VLM hidden-state positions (either the final feature grid for GR00T’s DiT head, or the per-layer KV cache for π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s flow-matching expert). Zeroing out 50% of image-token positions produces sharp, structured holes in the attention map that the pretrained action head is not trained to handle. SR drops by an average of ∼\sim18pp; the degradation is largest on long-horizon LIBERO-10 (−-34pp), consistent with the action head compounding errors from these holes across the 8-step action chunks. The large drop on dual-system VLAs is thus an architectural-sensitivity finding inherent to dense-attention action heads.

VLA-Cache adaptation.

VLA-Cache Xu and others [2025] reuses image-token KV entries across consecutive timesteps when inter-frame patch-wise visual similarity is high.

Hyperparameters. We use the original paper’s reported hyperparameters: per-patch cosine-similarity threshold τ=0.1\tau=0.1, reuse policy “cache if cosine≥1−τ\geq 1-\tau, else refresh”. We also swept τ∈{0.05,0.10,0.20}\tau\in\{0.05,0.10,0.20\} and report the best SR (τ=0.10\tau=0.10) in the main table; a tighter threshold (τ=0.05\tau{=}0.05) yielded higher SR at the cost of almost no latency reduction (<<5%).

Integration point. Identical refresh mask is applied to every transformer layer’s KV cache for image-token positions; text-token KVs are always refreshed. We do not modify the action head; it consumes the (partially cached) KV cache as-is.

Why the speedup ceiling is low. Because VLA-Cache still runs a full forward pass through the LLM backbone—only cached-position K/V are skipped—the latency reduction is bounded by the fraction of backbone compute spent on image-token K/V projections (roughly 15–20% on both VLAs). Observed per-step latency reduction is 14–17%, yielding a net 1.08×\times wall-clock speedup. This is the upper bound of the method on dual-system architectures; Latent Bridge exceeds it by replacing the backbone entirely on bridge steps, achieving 39–45% per-step reduction and 1.65–1.73×\times net speedup.

Amdahl ceiling: why token-pruning speedups shrink on dual-system VLAs.

The modest net speedup of FastV and VLA-Cache in Table 1 is not an implementation artifact but a structural consequence of Amdahl’s law applied to the dual-system latency breakdown.

On single-system VLAs (e.g., OpenVLA), the LLM backbone is the entire inference pipeline—the same LLM produces action tokens directly—so any reduction in LLM latency translates 1-to-1 into end-to-end speedup. In that setting, FastV and VLA-Cache each report roughly 1.3–1.5×1.3\text{--}1.5\times wall-clock speedup in their original papers.

On dual-system VLAs the same pruning only accelerates the first system (the VLM backbone), while the second system (the action head) runs unchanged at every step. Using our measured breakdown (Table 11), the backbone fraction of per-step sync cost is 63/90=70%63/90=70\% on GR00T and 46/76=60%46/76=60\% on π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Even if token pruning gave a 1.5×1.5\times local speedup on the backbone (its single-system ceiling), the per-step net speedup on dual-system would be bounded by Amdahl’s law at

1(1−p)+p/slocal=10.30+0.70/1.5≈1.30×(GR00T),≈1.23×(π0.5),\frac{1}{(1-p)+p/s_{\text{local}}}=\frac{1}{0.30+0.70/1.5}\approx 1.30\times\quad\text{(GR00T)},\qquad\approx 1.23\times\quad\text{($\pi_{0.5}$)},

and in practice the local speedup is well below 1.5×1.5\times on both backbones (VLA-Cache: ∼\sim15% backbone reduction == slocal≈1.18s_{\text{local}}\approx 1.18; FastV: similar). The observed 1.08×1.08\times net speedup for VLA-Cache in Table 1 tracks this bound.

Latent Bridge escapes this ceiling by replacing the backbone entirely on bridge steps: bridge step cost is 2–6 ms versus a 46–63 ms VLM backbone, a ≈\approx10–30×10\text{--}30\times local speedup at the backbone-step level. Even after amortizing over the remaining action-head cost and the mix of VLM and bridge steps within period ff, the net per-step latency drops to 46–49 ms on both VLAs—yielding the reported 1.65–1.73×1.65\text{--}1.73\times net wall-clock speedup, well beyond the Amdahl-bounded ceiling of token-pruning methods on dual-system architectures. This is the central architectural reason why delta prediction dominates token pruning in this setting: skipping a call is fundamentally cheaper than making an existing call faster.

Appendix I Qualitative Results

We present qualitative comparisons on three representative tasks spanning LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, and LIBERO-10. For each task, we show (i) agentview trajectory frames at four representative timesteps under Sync (ground truth), Latent Bridge (f=3f{=}3), and Feature Cache (Δt=0\Delta_{t}{=}0); and (ii) per-step KV cache cosine similarity to ground truth. All runs share the same initial environment state and random seed.

Across all cases, the Latent Bridge maintains near-unity cosine similarity to the ground-truth KV cache on non-VLM steps, producing trajectories visually indistinguishable from the Sync baseline. Feature Cache exhibits sawtooth degradation in KV fidelity between VLM refreshes, leading to compounding action errors and task failures.

Appendix J Limitations

State-in-prompt configurations.

For VLA variants that tokenize proprioceptive state into the language prompt (e.g., π0.5\pi_{0.5} with discrete_state_input=True), the bridge’s cached prefix KV carries stale state when reused across bridge steps, degrading performance. In our experiments, the ALOHA π0.5\pi_{0.5} model required fine-tuning with discrete_state_input=False (state routed through the action expert instead of the language prompt) to enable bridge compatibility. This limitation is specific to state-in-prompt designs and does not affect the standard LIBERO π0.5\pi_{0.5} or GR00T configurations.

Online DAgger requires a simulator.

Stage 3 of our pipeline requires deploying the bridge in simulation to collect DAgger data. For real-robot deployment, the bridge would need to be trained entirely offline on sync data (R0), potentially with augmented data generation. Our R0 bridges recover 93–96% of sync SR on LIBERO, suggesting R0-only training is viable when a simulator is unavailable.

Per-checkpoint training.

The bridge is specific to a given VLA checkpoint: changing the fine-tuned model requires retraining the bridge. Since bridge training is lightweight (2–4 hours on a single GPU), this adds modest overhead but limits “drop-in” deployment across frequently updated VLAs.

Episode-length side effect.

Bridge-driven rollouts are slightly longer than sync rollouts (+5–6% control steps on successful episodes) because the policy occasionally takes minor detours before task completion. This partially offsets per-step savings but is already accounted for in our reported net speedup numbers (1.65–1.73×\times).
